title: Workload Identity
summary: Workload identity gives a running process a verifiable identity so it can obtain short-lived cloud credentials without a stored secret. The mechanism relies on a trusted platform issuing a signed token that describes the workload, after which a provider's token service validates the token signature and claims against a trust policy and exchanges it for temporary credentials scoped to a role. Those claims are the real security boundary, because they bind the identity to attributes such as the cluster, namespace and service account, or the repository, branch and workflow that requested it. The pattern appears in container platforms, continuous integration jobs and service meshes, replacing static access keys stored in configuration files and environment variables. The mistake is writing a trust policy far broader than the workload it serves, for example trusting every repository in an organisation or every service account in a cluster, which lets anyone able to create a workload in that space assume the role. Long-lived keys left in place after migration are the other common gap.

beginner.definition: Workload identity is a way for a program to prove who it is without storing a password. The program runs inside a trusted platform, and that platform gives it a short lived pass. The cloud provider checks the pass and then hands over temporary keys. Nothing secret is written in the code, so there is nothing to steal from a file.
beginner.whyItMatters: Programs often carry long lived keys in their settings, and those keys leak through code, logs and old backups. A stolen key keeps working until someone notices and changes it, which may take months. Workload identity removes the key completely, because the program asks for a fresh pass each time. It also makes the audit trail clearer, since each action is tied to one specific program.
howItWorks: The platform where the code runs, such as a cluster or build system, creates a signed token for that program.
The token describes the program, for example which cluster namespace and which service account it uses.
The program sends the token to the cloud provider and asks for temporary access.
The provider checks the signature and compares the claims with a trust policy you wrote in advance.
If everything matches, the provider returns short lived credentials for one defined role.
The credentials expire quickly, so a copied token becomes useless within minutes or hours.
beginner.example: Imagine a large office where the canteen only serves people on shift. You do not carry a permanent key to the kitchen. Your manager confirms to the door system that you are working today. The door then gives you a pass for your shift only. When your shift ends, the pass stops working. Workload identity is that arrangement for programs. The platform confirms the program is real and running, and the cloud hands out a pass that expires. No permanent kitchen key ever leaves the building.
takeaways: Prefer short lived identity over stored keys, because there is no long term secret to leak.
Write narrow trust rules that name the exact program, cluster and namespace you expect.
Remove old keys after you move a program to workload identity, since forgotten keys stay dangerous.

objectives: Explain what a workload identity is and how it replaces stored secrets.
Describe how a signed token is exchanged for temporary cloud credentials.
Explain why the claims inside a trust policy matter for security.
Compare workload identity with long lived access keys from a risk point of view.
Describe how workload identity improves attribution in audit logs.
